questions.q: The list of approved vendors ___ been updated.
questions.why: The subject is 'list' (singular). 'Of approved vendors' is just a description.

questions.q: Neither the manager nor the analysts ___ aware of the change.
questions.why: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'analysts' (plural).

questions.q: Neither the analysts nor the manager ___ aware of the change.
questions.why: The nearer subject is 'manager' (singular), so 'was'.

questions.q: Each of the candidates ___ a strong portfolio.
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, even when followed by 'of the candidates'.
Used with 'its', the committee acts as one unit, so the verb is singular.

questions.q: Along with her two assistants, the director ___ attending the summit.
questions.why: 'Along with...' doesn't change the subject. The subject is 'the director'.

questions.q: There ___ several issues with the proposal.
questions.why: With 'there is/are', the verb agrees with what follows: 'several issues' (plural).

options: Every employee must submit their timesheet by Friday.
Every employees must submit their timesheet by Friday.
Every employee must submits their timesheet by Friday.
Every employee must submit there timesheet by Friday.
questions.why: 'Every' takes a singular noun; singular 'their' is accepted by major style guides.

questions.q: One of the reports that ___ submitted last week contains an error.
questions.why: 'That' refers to 'reports' (plural), so the verb in that clause is 'were'. The main verb 'contains' agrees with 'one'.

questions.q: The number of applicants ___ increased this year.
questions.why: 'The number of' is singular. ('A number of applicants have...' would be plural.)

questions.q: A number of employees ___ requested remote work.
questions.why: 'A number of' means 'several', so it takes a plural verb.

questions.q: Ten thousand dollars ___ a reasonable budget for the pilot.
questions.why: An amount of money treated as one sum takes a singular verb.

questions.q: Mathematics ___ a required subject for the program.
questions.why: Subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, economics) are singular when they name a field of study.

questions.q: Find the error: 'The quality of the products have improved since the new supplier was hired.'
questions.why: The subject is 'quality' (singular), so it should be 'has improved'.

questions.q: The CEO, as well as the board members, ___ expected to attend.
questions.why: 'As well as...' is extra information; the subject is 'the CEO'.

questions.q: Either the client or her lawyers ___ going to call us back.
questions.why: With either/or, match the nearer subject: 'lawyers' (plural).

questions.q: By the time the audit begins, we ___ all the documents.
questions.why: An action completed before a future point uses the future perfect.

questions.q: She ___ at the firm for ten years before she was promoted.
questions.why: Duration before another past event uses the past perfect.

questions.q: If I ___ about the delay, I would have informed the client.
questions.why: Third conditional (an unreal past): if + had + past participle.
Modal + have + past participle. 'Should of' is a common error for 'should've'.

options: The documents were laid on the desk.
The documents were lain on the desk.
The documents were layed on the desk.
The documents were lied on the desk.
questions.why: 'Lay' (to put) takes an object; its passive is 'were laid'.

questions.q: Yesterday the manager ___ down for an hour because of a headache.
questions.why: The past tense of 'lie' (to recline) is 'lay'.

questions.q: It is essential that every participant ___ the consent form.
questions.why: After 'essential that', formal English uses the subjunctive base form: 'sign'.

questions.q: The board recommended that the policy ___ revised.
questions.why: Subjunctive after 'recommended that': base form 'be'.

questions.q: We ___ the new software since January.
questions.why: An action that began in the past and continues now: present perfect continuous.
Begin – began – begun. After 'has', use the past participle 'begun'.

options: The price of materials has risen sharply.
The price of materials has rose sharply.
The price of materials has raised sharply.
The price of materials has rised sharply.
questions.why: Rise – rose – risen (no object). 'Raise' needs an object: 'They raised the price.'
'Raise' takes an object (its prices); past tense 'raised'.
It started before I arrived (two past events): past perfect.

questions.q: I look forward to ___ from you.
questions.why: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it's followed by -ing.

questions.q: The team ___ the deadline if they had started earlier.
questions.why: Third conditional result: would have + past participle.
Drink – drank – drunk. 'Has' needs the past participle 'drunk'.

options: The deadline is Friday, however, we may need an extension.
The deadline is Friday; however, we may need an extension.
The deadline is Friday however; we may need an extension.
The deadline is Friday: however we may need an extension.
questions.why: 'However' joining two independent clauses needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

options: Our offices are in Paris, France, Berlin, Germany, and Madrid, Spain.
Our offices are in Paris, France; Berlin, Germany; and Madrid, Spain.
Our offices are in Paris; France, Berlin; Germany, and Madrid; Spain.
Our offices are in: Paris, France, Berlin, Germany and Madrid, Spain.
questions.why: When list items contain commas, separate the items with semicolons.

options: The company changed it is logo.
questions.why: 'Its' is possessive. 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has'.

options: The employees' lounge is on the third floor.
The employee's lounge is on the third floor (shared by all staff).
The employees lounge's is on the third floor.
The employees's lounge is on the third floor.
questions.why: A lounge shared by many employees: plural possessive 'employees''.

options: The required documents are: a passport, a visa, and a photo.
Please bring three documents: a passport, a visa, and a photo.
Please bring: a passport, a visa, and a photo.
The documents: are a passport, a visa, and a photo.
questions.why: A colon must follow a complete sentence. Don't place one directly after a verb.

options: My manager who joined last year is very supportive.
My manager, who joined last year, is very supportive.
My manager, who joined last year is very supportive.
My manager who joined last year, is very supportive.
questions.why: You have one manager, so the clause is extra information and needs commas on both sides.

options: Employees, who arrive late, must sign in at reception.
Employees who arrive late must sign in at reception.
Employees who arrive late, must sign in at reception.
Employees, who arrive late must sign in at reception.
questions.why: The clause identifies which employees (essential), so no commas.
In American English, periods and commas go inside closing quotation marks.

options: The client approved the budget, so we began work.
The client approved the budget, we began work.
The client approved the budget; we began work.
After the client approved the budget, we began work.
questions.why: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.

options: We need a well-designed, user-friendly interface.
We need a well designed, user friendly interface.
We need a well-designed user-friendly, interface.
We need a well, designed user, friendly interface.
questions.why: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun; separate two equal adjectives with a comma.

questions.q: Which is correct in formal writing?
questions.why: After 'from', use 'to'. Use an en dash on its own, without 'from': 'the 2019–2022 project'.

options: If you need help please call me.
Please call me if you need help.
questions.why: An introductory if-clause is followed by a comma: 'If you need help, please call me.'
In formal American business letters, the salutation takes a colon (a comma is used in friendly letters).

options: The 1990's were a decade of growth.
The 1990s were a decade of growth.
The 1990s' were a decade of growth.
The 1990s's were a decade of growth.
questions.why: Decades are plural, not possessive: no apostrophe.

options: I have two concerns: cost and time.
I have two concerns; cost and time.
I have two concerns, cost, and time.
I have: two concerns cost and time.
questions.why: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the em dash correctly?
questions.why: Em dashes come in pairs around an interrupting phrase in mid-sentence.

questions.q: The new policy will ___ all departments.
questions.why: 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'influence'.

questions.q: The new manager hopes to ___ real change.
questions.why: 'Effect' as a verb means 'to bring about'. A rare but formal use.

questions.q: Please ___ that all files are backed up.
questions.why: 'Ensure' = make certain. 'Insure' = cover with insurance. 'Assure' = tell someone confidently.

questions.q: The ___ reason for the delay was a supply shortage.
questions.why: 'Principal' = main. 'Principle' = a rule or belief.
Traditionally, the whole comprises its parts: no 'of'. ('Is composed of' is also correct.)

questions.q: There were ___ errors in this draft than in the last one.
questions.why: Errors are countable: 'fewer'.

options: Bring several items, e.g., a laptop and a charger.
Bring several items, i.e., a laptop and a charger (examples).
Bring several items, ie a laptop.
Bring several items, eg., a laptop.
questions.why: 'e.g.' = for example. 'i.e.' = that is (restates exactly).
'Complement' = complete or go well with. 'Compliment' = praise.

questions.q: To ___ should the invoice be addressed?
questions.why: After a preposition, use 'whom'.

options: Irregardless of the cost, we will proceed.
Regardless of the cost, we will proceed.
Irregardless the cost, we will proceed.
Regardless the cost of, we will proceed.
questions.why: 'Regardless' is standard. 'Irregardless' is considered nonstandard in formal writing.

questions.q: The proposal was approved, ___ we will start next week.
questions.why: 'So' links cause and result after a comma.

questions.q: All staff must ___ the new safety guidelines.
questions.why: The verb 'adhere' is always followed by 'to'.

questions.q: He was ___ by the complex instructions.
questions.why: -ed adjectives describe how someone feels; -ing adjectives describe what causes it.

options: Please advise me of any changes.
Please advice me of any changes.
Please adviced me of any changes.
Please advices me of any changes.
questions.why: 'Advise' is the verb; 'advice' is the noun.
'Accept' = agree to. 'Except' = excluding.

questions.q: The firm is ___ to strict regulations.
questions.why: 'Subject to' = governed by. 'Subjected to' means made to undergo something (often unpleasant).

options: The role requires planning, organizing, and to lead a team.
The role requires planning, organizing, and leading a team.
The role requires to plan, organizing, and leading a team.
The role requires plan, to organize, and leading a team.
questions.why: All items in a list should share the same form (-ing).

questions.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
options: After reviewing the data, the analyst found an error.
After reviewing the data, an error was found.
The analyst found an error after reviewing the data.
An error was found after the analyst reviewed the data.
questions.why: Who reviewed the data? Not 'an error'. The modifier has no correct subject.

options: Because of the delay in shipping.
The budget was approved despite the delay.
Which caused the delay in shipping.
questions.why: The others are dependent clauses or phrases that cannot stand alone.

options: Not only did sales increase, but profits also rose.
Not only sales increased, but profits also rose.
Not only did sales increased, but profits also rose.
Not only sales did increase, but profits rose also.
questions.why: When 'not only' starts a sentence, invert the subject and helper: 'did sales increase'.

options: Rarely we see such strong results.
Rarely do we see such strong results.
Rarely we do see such strong results.
Rarely seeing we such strong results.
questions.why: Negative adverbs at the start (rarely, seldom, never) trigger inversion.

questions.q: Which places 'only' to mean 'no one except the manager approved it'?
options: The manager only approved the budget.
Only the manager approved the budget.
The manager approved only the budget.
The manager approved the budget only.
questions.why: Place 'only' directly before the word it limits.

options: She told her colleague that she had made a mistake.
She told her colleague, 'I made a mistake.'
She told her that she had made a mistake.
She told her colleague that her mistake was made.
questions.why: The first version is ambiguous: whose mistake? Direct speech removes the confusion.

options: The reason is because the server crashed.
The reason is that the server crashed.
The reason why is because the server crashed.
The reason is due to because the server crashed.
questions.why: 'The reason is that...' avoids redundancy ('reason' already means 'because').

options: The new system is more faster than the old one.
The new system is faster than the old one.
The new system is fastest than the old one.
The new system is more fast than the old one.
questions.why: One-syllable adjectives take -er; never combine 'more' with -er.

options: She is one of the most talented engineers who has ever worked here.
She is one of the most talented engineers who have ever worked here.
She is one of the most talented engineer who have ever worked here.
She is one of the more talented engineer who has worked here.
questions.why: 'Who' refers to 'engineers' (plural), so 'have'.

options: Our prices are lower than our competitors.
Our prices are lower than those of our competitors.
Our prices are lower then our competitors.
Our prices are lower compared with competitors prices.
questions.why: Compare prices with prices, not prices with competitors.

options: Between you and I, the plan won't work.
Between you and me, the plan won't work.
Between yourself and I, the plan won't work.
Between you and myself, the plan won't work.
questions.why: Prepositions take object pronouns: 'me'.

options: The manager asked whether we had finished the report.
The manager asked had we finished the report.
The manager asked whether had we finished the report.
The manager asked did we finish the report?
questions.why: Reported questions use 'whether/if' and normal word order, with no question mark.

options: Hardly had we started when the power failed.
Hardly we had started when the power failed.
Hardly had we started than the power failed.
Hardly we started when the power failed.
questions.why: 'Hardly ... when' with inversion: 'Hardly had we started when...'

questions.q: Which sentence avoids a misplaced modifier?
options: We sent the brochure to clients printed on recycled paper.
We sent clients the brochure printed on recycled paper.
Printed on recycled paper, we sent the brochure to clients.
We sent, printed on recycled paper, clients the brochure.
questions.why: Keep 'printed on recycled paper' next to 'brochure'.

options: Whom do you think will win the contract?
Who do you think will win the contract?
Whom do you think it will win the contract?
Who you think will win the contract?
questions.why: Ignore 'do you think': 'Who will win?' (he will win).

options: Due to the fact that the server failed, we lost data.
Because the server failed, we lost data.
In view of the fact that the server failed, data was lost by us.
Owing to the fact of the server failing, we lost data.
questions.why: Replace wordy phrases like 'due to the fact that' with 'because'.

options: We will meet at 10 a.m. in the morning.
We will meet at 10 a.m. o'clock in the morning.
We will meet at 10 in the a.m.
questions.why: 'a.m.' already means 'in the morning'.

questions.q: Which is most appropriate for a formal email?
options: Hi team, I'm following up on yesterday's meeting.
questions.why: Professional but friendly, with no slang or repeated punctuation.

questions.q: Which is the best active-voice version of 'Mistakes were made by the accounting team'?
options: Made were mistakes by the team.
The mistakes the team made were made.
questions.why: Active voice names the doer clearly and directly.
An outcome is already final. Other examples: 'past history', 'end result', 'advance planning'.

questions.q: Which is the most professional sign-off?
questions.why: 'Best regards' and 'Kind regards' are standard professional closings.

questions.q: Which sentence is the most concise?
options: At this point in time, we are unable to proceed.
At the present moment in time, we are not able to proceed.
Currently, at this time, we cannot proceed.
questions.why: 'At this point in time' is wordy for 'now'.

questions.q: Which is correct in formal writing?
questions.why: 'Unique' means one of a kind; traditional usage avoids grading it.

options: Could you please send me the file?
You need to send me the file.
questions.why: A question with 'could you please' is polite and professional.

options: At the end of the day, we need results.
We need results by the end of the quarter.
Let's think outside the box for results.
It is what it is; we need results.
questions.why: Specific language beats clichés like 'at the end of the day'.

options: We made a decision to conduct an investigation.
A decision was made to conduct an investigation.
Our decision was the conduct of an investigation.
questions.why: Turn noun phrases ('make a decision') back into verbs ('decide').

options: Each manager should submit his report.
Each manager should submit their report.
Each manager should submit her or his reports'.
Each managers should submit their report.
questions.why: Singular 'they/their' is accepted by APA, Chicago and AP styles.

questions.q: Which is the best subject line for a work email?
options: Q3 budget review: decision needed by Friday
questions.why: A good subject line is specific and states any action or deadline.
Avoid informal words like 'gonna' and 'kinda' in professional writing.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the passive voice appropriately?
options: The ball was kicked by me.
A decision was made by me to quit.
The email was written by me yesterday.
questions.why: The passive is fine when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or obvious.

questions.q: Which is correct in a formal report?
options: The data shows a clear trend.
The data show a clear trend.
Both are acceptable; 'data show' is more traditional in academic writing.
questions.why: 'Data' is treated as plural in traditional academic style and as a mass noun in everyday and business use.
